Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis traditionally assigned to Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QGenb in DJD XII (Davila). Its editor suspected it may instead derive from Wadi Murabba'at: its leather is coarse and poorly prepared, unusual for Qumran, its script is typologically late, and no fragment of it was identified among photographs from the controlled Cave 4 excavations. Its best-preserved portion is a relatively intact column covering the opening of Genesis 1 (Genesis 1:1-25a in the Lyon summary), with further scattered remains from Genesis 2, 4 and 5. The surviving text is essentially identical to the Masoretic Text; one exhibit summary notes a single minor spelling difference in Genesis 1:15.
Significance: An early witness to the stability of the Genesis text: a copy made around the turn of the era already agrees with the Masoretic Text that underlies modern Hebrew Bibles, including at the creation account in Genesis 1. Its value is as a textual witness, not as a complete Genesis scroll — only scattered verses survive, so it proves nothing about chapters it does not preserve.

Description: A lengthy Hebrew copy of Exodus in palaeo-Hebrew script, published in DJD IX (Skehan, Ulrich, Sanderson). The original scroll occupied about 45 columns, spanning Exodus 6:25 to 37:16. It is poorly preserved in detail — no column survives entirely undamaged and many columns are represented only by scattered fragments — but its overall range and word-count (over 1,000 words preserved) make it the most extensive Exodus manuscript from Qumran.
Significance: The key witness to the expansive, pre-Samaritan form of Exodus: it attests harmonistic expansions similar to those in the Samaritan Pentateuch, showing that an expanded Exodus text circulated in the late Second Temple period alongside the shorter tradition that became the Masoretic Text. It therefore proves textual plurality in this period, not a single uniform Exodus text.

DateApprox: c. late 2nd century BC - 1st century AD (dating debated)
Description: A Hebrew Leviticus scroll in palaeo-Hebrew script, discovered in Cave 11 in January 1956 and held first at the Rockefeller Museum, where it was photographed in 1956 and again in detail by the Israel Antiquities Authority in 1970. It survives as the lower portion of its final columns, on parchment (kid leather, about 100 cm long as preserved), plus eighteen small fragments from earlier chapters. The main sheet covers Leviticus 22-27; the fragments extend coverage to Leviticus 4, 10, 11, 13-17 and 18-22. A single experienced scribe wrote it, with dots as word-dividers and letters suspended from ruled lines.
ImageCredit: Shai Halevi on behalf of the Israel Antiquities Authority — CC BY-SA 4.0
Significance: The most substantial Leviticus manuscript from Qumran and a showcase for the ancient palaeo-Hebrew script, the script formerly used for Torah scrolls in pre-exilic Israel. It is considered a primary witness to the proto-Masoretic text of Leviticus, making it a central witness for Leviticus textual history and for the laws of sacrifice, atonement, festivals and holiness in Leviticus 22-27.

Description: A lengthy Hebrew copy of Numbers from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XII (Jastram). Remains of 27 columns survive, covering Numbers 11-36 in fragments, written in early Herodian semiformal Hebrew script. A few lines are written in red ink. It is one of only a handful of Qumran biblical manuscripts with over 1,000 words preserved.
Significance: The fullest Numbers witness from Qumran, and a pre-Samaritan (expansionist) text: many of its variants agree with the Samaritan Pentateuch against the Masoretic Text, demonstrating that differing versions of Numbers circulated in the Second Temple period.

Description: A small but exceptionally well-preserved parchment manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, published by Sidnie White Crawford (JBL 109/2, 1990) as the All Souls Deuteronomy. It consists of two sheets and six columns — four complete columns and two partially damaged — with columns 2-6 on one continuous sheet of parchment. In the manuscript the passages appear in the order Deuteronomy 8:5-10, then Deuteronomy 5:1-6:1, an ordering that, with the blank space at the bottom of column 1, is the main reason scholars argue it is an excerpted/liturgical collection rather than a regular Deuteronomy scroll (an alternative explanation is incorrect repair of the scroll). Its script is unusually tiny, with waw and yod almost indistinguishable, and its orthography is much fuller than that of either the Masoretic Text or the Samaritan Pentateuch.
Significance: Crawford calls it the best-preserved of all the Deuteronomy manuscripts from Cave 4, and it preserves the Decalogue (Deuteronomy 5) in full. Its Decalogue generally follows Deuteronomy but is harmonised toward the Exodus parallel, including one variant unique to this manuscript: the addition of the Exodus reason for the Sabbath commandment. Press reports have called it the oldest complete copy of the Ten Commandments; that title is disputed — the Nash Papyrus (c. 150-100 BC) is older, and 4Q41 itself may be a liturgical excerpt rather than a Torah scroll — so the entry does not repeat the press claim as fact.

Description: Fragments of Joshua from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QJosha (DJD 14). The surviving text spans five chapters (5, 6, 7, 8, 10), including the fall of Jericho material (chapter 6), the Achan episode (chapter 7), and the southern campaign (chapter 10). The Leon Levy record shows 44 images of this manuscript.
Significance: The fullest Qumran witness to Joshua. Its most discussed feature is the position of Joshua 8:34–35 before 5:2, showing that the blessings-and-curses passage circulated in a different place in the book; Ulrich cautions that it is not certain the altar-building verses (8:30–31) preceded them, since that text would fall in an unpreserved part of the preceding column. Its text shows variations in wording and omissions against the Masoretic Text, with some readings aligning with the Greek text.

Description: Fragments of Judges from Qumran Cave 1, published as 1QJudg (DJD 1, pp. 62-64, Barthelemy 1955). The surviving text covers parts of chapters 6, 8 and 9, including the Gideon and Abimelech material. The Leon Levy record lists Site Qumran Cave 1, Manuscript Type Biblical Compositions, Composition Type Scripture, Language Hebrew, Script Square, Period Hellenistic-Roman, Material Parchment, and 4 images. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.
Significance: One of three Qumran copies of Judges (with 4QJudga, covering chapter 6, and 4QJudgb, covering chapters 19 and 21), and the fullest of the three. Its text is close to the Masoretic Text. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.

Description: Fragments of Ruth from Qumran Cave 2, published as 2QRutha. The surviving text spans three chapters (2, 3 and 4): Ruth's gleaning and her meeting with Boaz (chapter 2), the threshing-floor scene (chapter 3), and the redemption transaction at the gate (chapter 4). The Leon Levy record shows 38 images of this manuscript. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.
Significance: The fullest Qumran witness to Ruth by chapter span and coverage (chapters 2–4). Ruth copies at Qumran show only slight variations from the Masoretic Text. The earlier Hasmonean copy 4Q104 preserves the continuous opening of the book (Ruth 1:1–12), and 4Q105 preserves Ruth 1:1–6, 12–15.

Description: The most extensive Samuel scroll from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QSama (DJD 17, pp. 1-216, 217). In antiquity Samuel was one work, so this single scroll counts once and covers both 1 and 2 Samuel. It survives in 11 partially preserved columns and some 165 fragments with identified contents plus unidentified fragments, at 47 lines per column and about 32.7 cm high including the bottom margin. Only 8 scribal corrections are reported; the scroll was worn in antiquity and reinforced with papyrus pieces glued on the back plus 2 leather patches. The Leon Levy record lists Material Parchment, Script Square, Period Hellenistic-Roman, and 726 images.
Significance: The most important Qumran witness to Samuel. Many of its readings differ from the Masoretic Text but agree with the Septuagint / Old Greek. Its most famous contribution is the longer Nahash paragraph before 1 Samuel 11:1, attested by 4QSama — where the scribe first skipped part of it by homoioteleuton and then inserted the missing words between the lines — and by Josephus, Antiquities 6.68–71; the paragraph is absent from the Masoretic Text. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.

Description: A papyrus scroll of Kings from Qumran Cave 6, published as 6QpapKgs (DJD 3). In antiquity Kings was one work, so this single scroll counts once and covers both 1 and 2 Kings. It is poorly preserved on 94 papyrus fragments, of which only 17 have been identified. Its script is described as archaic, written in a less professional manner but with few errors. The Leon Levy record shows 170 images of this manuscript. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.
Significance: The only one of the three Qumran Kings manuscripts that covers both 1 and 2 Kings (4Q54 and 5Q2 preserve 1 Kings only), and the fullest by coverage. It carries multiple literary variants, some found in other textual witnesses; Tigchelaar notes it was written in a less professional manner but with few errors, while 4Q54 was a nonprofessional copy on substandard material.

Description: The only identified Qumran copy of Chronicles, from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QChr / 4QChron. It is a single fragment with letters from two columns, the first column unidentified and the second offering a few letters from four verses (2 Chronicles 28:27-29:3) — the death of Ahaz and the accession of Hezekiah. In antiquity Chronicles was one work, but only 2 Chronicles text survives in this manuscript, so Work and RelatedBooks list 2 Chronicles only.
Significance: The sole Qumran witness to Chronicles, and therefore the best-preserved by default. No 1 Chronicles passage survives at Qumran in any identified manuscript. Its surviving text is consistent with the Masoretic Text tradition. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation. Only a few letters survive from each of the four verses, so the identification rests on a small amount of text.

Description: The only identified Qumran copy of the Ezra-Nehemiah work, from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QEzra (DJD 16, pp. 291-93, pl. 38). Three fragments preserve bits and pieces of Ezra chapters 4, 5 and 6, including the Aramaic section of Ezra (Ezra 4:9-6:5 is in Aramaic in the biblical text itself, and is preserved here in Aramaic — this is the original language of that passage, not a translation). In antiquity Ezra-Nehemiah was one work, and the DJD list labels this manuscript '4QEzra (= Ezra-Nehemiah)'; that label is about the ancient combined work, NOT evidence that Nehemiah text survives in it. Work and RelatedBooks therefore list Ezra only.
Significance: The sole Qumran witness to the Ezra-Nehemiah work, and therefore the best-preserved by default. Its surviving text is consistent with the Masoretic Text tradition. No Nehemiah verse text survives in any identified Qumran manuscript, so Nehemiah has no entry of its own; an earlier reported Nehemiah fragment was challenged as a forgery.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Job from Qumran Cave 4, written in Hasmonean script on thin, well-prepared skin, arranged stichometrically in narrow columns. Only a few fragments survive; editors estimate that a complete copy of Job in this format would have run to about 72 columns. It is one of six Job manuscripts from Qumran (2Q15, 4Q99, 4Q100, 4Q101, 4Q157, 11Q10), and the only Hebrew copy with more than small fragments preserved.
Significance: One of the oldest textual witnesses to the Hebrew book of Job, which reached its final redaction in the 3rd century BC. Its value is as an early Hebrew witness to the text of Job's speeches and Elihu's speeches (chapters 31-37) centuries before the medieval Masoretic manuscripts; its fragmentary condition means it cannot settle the book's textual history on its own, and its few corrections away from the Masoretic Text are noted rather than treated as a separate edition.

Description: The most substantial and best-preserved Psalms manuscript among the Dead Sea Scrolls: five sheets of leather still sewn together, about 4.25 metres long in its surviving body (28 columns, plus separate fragments A-F), discovered in Cave 11 in February 1956 and first unrolled in 1961. It contains 49 compositions. It is not a copy of the whole Psalter: it runs chiefly through Psalms 101-150, in an order different from the Masoretic Psalter, and it mixes canonical psalms with compositions not in the Masoretic Psalter.
PreservedPassages: Chiefly Psalms 101-150 in a non-Masoretic order (with gaps), plus Psalm 93, Psalm 151, Syriac Psalms 154-155, Sirach 51, the Plea for Deliverance, the Hymn to the Creator, the Apostrophe to Zion, David's Compositions, and David's Last Words (2 Samuel 23:7)
Significance: Shows that in the 1st century AD the order and contents of the later part of the Psalter were not yet fixed: 11Q5 arranges Psalms 101-150 differently from the Masoretic Text and adds psalms known from the Syriac tradition (151, 154, 155), Sirach 51, and previously unknown hymns, alongside a prose passage crediting David with 4,050 compositions. At the same time it confirms that most of these psalms were already circulating in Hebrew long before the medieval manuscripts, and its strong Davidic emphasis fits the Qumran community's messianic hopes. It is a liturgical collection, not a straight copy of the Masoretic Psalter, and must not be presented as one.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Proverbs from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script. It is the largest Qumran Proverbs copy: the published statistical count gives it about 126 words against about 42 for 4Q102 (4QProva, Proverbs 1:27-33; 2:1). The surviving verses come from the collections of individual proverbs in chapters 13-15, with two further verses from chapter 7 whose identification is marked uncertain in the published list.
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to Proverbs, about a thousand years older than the medieval Masoretic manuscripts. The surviving text stands close to the Masoretic Text, with only minor variation in the published count, so its chief value is confirming the early stability of these proverb collections rather than revealing a different edition of the book.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Ecclesiastes (Qohelet) from Qumran Cave 4, among the oldest Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran. The surviving text covers parts of chapters 5-7, including the well-known saying that sorrow is better than laughter (Ecclesiastes 7). It is the larger of the two Qumran Ecclesiastes copies: the published count gives it about 125 words against about 21 for 4Q110 (4QQohb, Ecclesiastes 1:10-15).
ImageCredit: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin — CC BY-SA 4.0
Significance: Pushes the Hebrew text of Ecclesiastes back to the mid-2nd century BC, centuries before the medieval manuscripts, and shows the book already in circulation in essentially its familiar form. Its variants against the Masoretic Text are minor in character; its importance is its age and its confirmation of the book's early transmission, not a rival text of Ecclesiastes.

Description: Three fragments (four columns) of a Hebrew copy of the Song of Solomon from Qumran Cave 4, in early Herodian script. The copy is selective: it omits Song of Solomon 3:6-8 and 4:4-7 and ends at 5:1, so it is an excerpted or anthologised copy rather than a complete book scroll. Scholars have debated its use: Emmanuel Tov at one point argued it was a liturgical text, later revised that to a text for private use, and then abstained from identifying its use, a position other scholars have also reached.
Significance: One of only four Qumran copies of the Song (4Q106, 4Q107, 4Q108, 6Q6), together preserving about 47 of the book's 117 verses. It confirms the Song was already being copied in Hebrew around the turn of the era, while its omissions and its ending at 5:1 show that at least one Qumran copy circulated the Song in a selective form. Small differences from the Masoretic Text, including word order, are preserved in its fragments.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Lamentations from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script, dated c. 30-1 BC. It preserves the opening chapter of Lamentations (chapter 1, with the pe/ayin verses in swapped order, 17 before 16, in the published contents) and one verse of chapter 2. It is one of four Lamentations manuscripts from Qumran (3Q3, 4Q111, 5Q6, 5Q7).
Significance: The fullest Lamentations witness at Qumran by published word count (about 193 words, against about 141 for 5Q6). It is also the most variant of the Qumran Lamentations copies against the Masoretic Text: in the published statistical count it shows 37 variants, and recent study argues that most of its differences are deliberate scribal creations rather than simple copying errors. It therefore shows the text of Lamentations still fluid in the 1st century BC, even though the great stability of most of the Masoretic tradition is also visible across the Qumran copies as a group.

CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book)
Description: One of the seven scrolls first found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947. Written on 17 sheets of stitched parchment, about 734 cm (24 feet) long, in 54 columns. It contains the whole Book of Isaiah in the order familiar from modern Bibles, apart from a few small damaged portions. Palaeography places the handwriting at about 150-125 BC (Tov); radiocarbon results also fall before the time of Jesus, and c. 125 BC is the round figure usually given.
Significance: The only Qumran biblical scroll preserved almost in its entirety, and the oldest known complete copy of Isaiah, roughly 1,000 years older than the medieval Masoretic manuscripts known before 1947. It agrees overwhelmingly with the Masoretic Text: the differences, numbering in the thousands, are mostly spelling and grammar, with only a small number affecting the sense of a line. It therefore shows both careful transmission over a millennium and that ancient copying was done by human scribes.

Description: The longest surviving copy of Jeremiah from Qumran, published in DJD XV (E. Tov, 'Jeremiah', in Qumran Cave 4, X: The Prophets, 1997, pp. 145-207, covering 4Q70, 4Q71, 4Q72, 4Q72a, 4Q72b). It survives only as fragments, but they span chapters 4 to 33, including the cup-of-wrath passage in chapter 25 and the restoration chapters 30-31. It is a proto-Masoretic copy: it follows the longer Masoretic order and text.
Significance: Together with 4QJera it proves that the longer Masoretic form of Jeremiah already existed in Hebrew in the Second Temple period. The shorter form behind the Greek Septuagint (about one-seventh shorter, with the oracles against the nations in a different place) is separately attested in Hebrew by 4QJerb and 4QJerd. Both editions therefore circulated in Hebrew side by side at Qumran; the difference is a real textual history, not a later Greek trimming of the Hebrew.

Description: The broadest surviving copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (J. E. Sanderson, 'Ezekiel', in Qumran Cave 4, X: The Prophets, 1997, pp. 209-220; 4Q73 at pp. 209-214, against 4Q74 at pp. 215-218 and 4Q75 at pp. 219-220). It survives as fragments from four separated passages: chapters 10, 11, 23, and 41 - the temple vision (chapters 10-11), the parable of Oholibah (chapter 23), and the temple measurements (chapter 41). The DJD editor Sanderson describes its hand as late Hasmonaean, while the Cave 4 list gives it as Herodian.
Significance: A proto-Masoretic witness that agrees substantially with the Masoretic Text of Ezekiel, including in the temple-vision and temple-measurement passages. Its value is as an early, pre-Christian Hebrew witness to the text of Ezekiel: it shows the book circulating in essentially the form later preserved in the Masoretic tradition, well before the medieval codices.

Description: Described in the BASOR preliminary edition as 'the most extensively preserved scroll' of Daniel from Qumran (Ulrich, Part 1; 4QDanb and 4QDanc, the other two substantially preserved Cave 4 copies, followed as Part 2). It survives as fragments spanning Daniel 1 to 11. The preserved text follows the book's own language pattern: Hebrew in chapter 1 and from chapter 8 onward, Aramaic in the middle section (the preserved Aramaic portion runs from Daniel 2:9 through 7:28 in this copy). Portions within the ranges listed are incomplete; this is a fragmentary scroll, not a continuous text.
Significance: The widest single Qumran witness to Daniel, and the clearest single-copy proof that Daniel's Hebrew-Aramaic-Hebrew structure already existed in a first-century BC Hebrew/Aramaic copy. It agrees in substance with the Masoretic Text. It is NOT the oldest Daniel copy (that distinction belongs to 4QDanc, 4Q114, late 2nd century BC, preserving Daniel 10-11); its claim is extent, not age. Across all eight Qumran Daniel manuscripts every chapter except Daniel 12 is represented; Daniel 12:10 is quoted as Scripture in the Florilegium (4Q174), so the absence of chapter 12 from the surviving Daniel fragments is not evidence the book lacked it at Qumran.

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum (and, questionably, Habakkuk). The most extensive Qumran manuscript of the Twelve Minor Prophets: a single Hebrew scroll, originally containing the whole Twelve collection, now surviving in many fragments. Only about 916 words can still be attributed to biblical text. The scribe copied carefully in an early Herodian book hand from the last third of the 1st century BC and corrected himself in nine cases. It does NOT contain Haggai or Malachi in its surviving portions. Note: a possible Habakkuk 2:4 fragment in this scroll is identified only with a question mark in the scholarly summary and is not counted here as a Habakkuk copy.
RelatedBooks: Hosea; Joel; Amos; Obadiah; Jonah; Micah; Nahum; Zephaniah; Zechariah
Significance: Textually important against the Masoretic Text: not counting reconstructed variants, 69 cases of variation between the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and 4QXIIg are preserved; 4QXIIg agrees with the Masoretic Text 15 times and against it 54 times (44 clear readings, a 4.80% deviation among 916 identifiable words), and also attests 39 non-aligned readings. Its orthography is slightly more plene than the Masoretic Text and uses some Qumran spellings. For Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah and Nahum it is the best-preserved Qumran biblical copy; for Habakkuk it is only a questionable single-verse fragment (see Description).
Work: Hosea; Joel; Amos; Obadiah; Jonah; Micah; Nahum; Zephaniah; Zechariah

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Joel only. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets scroll from Qumran Cave 4, surviving in fragments. Its surviving portions cover Hosea, Joel, Amos, Zephaniah and a questionable Malachi fragment. One summary describes it as containing many scribal mistakes but also very many original readings. Note: a possible Malachi 3:6-7 fragment in this scroll is identified only with a question mark and is not counted here as a Malachi copy. A possible Amos 1:1 fragment is likewise identified only with a question mark and is not counted here.
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Joel: its Joel coverage (Joel 1:10-20; 2:1, 8-23; 3:6, 8-10, 12-19, 21 in English numbering) is substantially larger than 4Q82's Joel coverage. It also preserves a large block of Hosea 4 and Amos 3 and 7, useful for checking the Masoretic Text, but it is not best for Hosea or Amos (both: 4Q82) or Zephaniah (4Q77) or Malachi (4Q76).

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Zephaniah and Haggai. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets scroll from Qumran Cave 4, dated 150-125 BC, surviving in fragments. Its largest fragment preserves the bottom edge of the manuscript, which helps determine the manuscript's dimensions and reconstruct it. It shows the Twelve Prophets written as one continuous book at Qumran.
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1-2; 2:13-15; 3:19-20) and of Haggai (Haggai 1:1-2; 2:2-4, five verses, against 4Q80's four Haggai verses, and the older of the two Haggai copies). Zephaniah's themes of judgment and redemption and Haggai's call to rebuild the temple after 586 BC are both present in this early copy.

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Zechariah only. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets scroll from Qumran Cave 4, dated 75-50 BC, surviving in fragments. Its surviving portions are almost exclusively from Zechariah, with a short Haggai section at the end of Haggai 2.
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Zechariah: it preserves parts of Zechariah 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 12, far more than 4Q76 (Zechariah 14:18 only) or 4Q82 (Zechariah 10-12 fragments). Its text is described as of a textual type related to the Septuagint. For Haggai it is the runner-up, not the best: Haggai 2:18-21 (four verses) against 4Q77's Haggai 1:1-2; 2:2-4 (five verses).

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Malachi only. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, dated c. 150-125 BC (semicursive hand, c. 150-100 BC in one palaeographic discussion; described as pre-Qumranic, c. 150 BC, in a 2015 study). It preserves a substantial Malachi section (Malachi 2:10 to the end of the book), a single Zechariah verse, and Jonah fragments as published in DJD XV. Note: Jonah fragments once attributed to this scroll in DJD XV are disputed by a later study, which argues the composition following Malachi was in all likelihood not Jonah; they are not counted here as a Jonah copy. The Zechariah attribution itself rests on a few letters on a single small fragment and has been questioned (the letters could also come from Jonah 4:10-11).
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Malachi by a wide margin: Malachi 2:10-4:6 (English numbering) survives here, including the closing Elijah passage (Malachi 4:5-6, Hebrew 3:23-24), against only a questionable Malachi 3:6-7 fragment in 4Q78. It is also important for the history of the Twelve as a collection: a 2015 study argues it probably contained only three or four of the shortest books, not all twelve, and that Malachi was followed by another composition that was in all likelihood NOT Jonah — so Malachi was not always the last book in a Twelve scroll, and the Twelve could be copied in sets as well as as a single collection.
